meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'First, we will take Eastern Europe, then the masses of Asia, then we will encircle the United States which will be the last bastion of capitalism. We will not have to attack. It will fall like an overripe fruit into our hands'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lenin. This Cold War 'overripe fruit' quote apparently first appeared in 1954 US Senate testimony, and nobody has found it in Lenin's writings.

answer.label: Not Vladimir Lenin — a Cold War fabrication
answer.authorName: Unknown (first circulated in 1950s American anti-communist circles)
answer.authorDates: Earliest known use: U.S. Senate subcommittee hearing record, June 17, 1954
answer.sourceLine: Nobody has found this in any of Lenin’s writings. Researchers at Stanford and the Library of Congress Slavic Room tried to authenticate it and failed. The earliest use we have found is in the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee’s published hearings, Strategy and Tactics of World Communism (1954) ↗. On June 17, 1954, J. Anthony Marcus, president of the Institute of Foreign Trade, put it into the record, crediting it to “volume X, Collected Works by Lenin, page 172.” The Soviet defector Nicholas Goncharoff repeated it to the same subcommittee on July 15, 1954. Boller & George’s They Never Said It (1989) ↗ says Goncharoff “apparently made the first use” of it, but the hearing record shows Marcus using it a month earlier. From there it spread through American anti-communist circles.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: No. The Overstreets found nothing like it in Lenin’s Selected Works, and Stanford researchers and the Library of Congress Slavic Room curator could not authenticate it (Boller & George).

J. Anthony Marcus, statement and testimony before the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, June 17, 1954 (Strategy and Tactics of World Communism, Part 2, pp. 131, 139). Nicholas Goncharoff repeated it to the subcommittee on July 15, 1954 (Part 4, p. 214).
Congressional Record — Appendix, extension of remarks dated July 2, 1960 (Rep. Charles S. Gubser, “The Communist Conspiracy”)
They Never Said It (Oxford University Press, 1989), pp. 70–72

source.excerpt: The Communist master plan for world conquest was stated by Lenin in these words, “First we will take Eastern Europe, then the masses of Asia, then we will encircle the United States, which will be the last bastion of capitalism. We will not have to attack. It will fall like an overripe fruit into our hands.”
trail: 1954: On June 17, J. Anthony Marcus, president of the Institute of Foreign Trade, put the line into the record of the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee twice, in his prepared statement and again in his testimony, crediting it to “volume X, Collected Works by Lenin, page 172” (Strategy and Tactics of World Communism, Part 2, pp. 131, 139 ↗). On July 15 the Russian defector Nicholas Goncharoff repeated it to the same subcommittee (Part 4, p. 214). Boller & George ↗ say Goncharoff “apparently made the first use” of it and date his testimony July 14; the hearing record shows Marcus a month earlier and dates Goncharoff’s session July 15. Wikiquote ↗ adds that Cardinal Francis Spellman used it in his speech to the 1954 American Legion National Convention.

1958: The line appeared in the John Birch Society’s Blue Book. Ex-Communist Louis F. Budenz then called it one of the “many questionable quotations from Lenin and Stalin that are floating around in ill-informed anti-Communist circles” (They Never Said It, pp. 70–72 ↗).
1960: Rep. Charles S. Gubser put it into the Congressional Record Appendix ↗, calling it “the Communist master plan for world conquest” as “stated by Lenin.”

1988: Asked by Soviet journalist Valentin Zorin which works of Lenin the quotations came from, President Reagan answered, “I don’t think I could recall and specify,” then paraphrased the overripe-fruit line again (American Presidency Project, May 20, 1988 ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is a speech Rep. Charles S. Gubser of California gave on Memorial Day 1960. It appears in the Congressional Record Appendix as an extension of remarks dated July 2, 1960. It shows how the line was used as if it were genuine, but it is not a Lenin source. The text was reassembled from a multi-column OCR scan.

author.name: Vladimir Lenin
author.heading: About Vladimir Lenin
author.metaLine: 1870–1924 · Russian revolutionary & founder of the Soviet state
author.bio: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin led the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 and headed the Soviet government until he died in January 1924. His writings fill a 45-volume English Collected Works. Nobody has found the “overripe fruit” strategy line in them, and it is one of many fake Lenin quotes that circulated in the United States during the Cold War.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: This line has been a Cold War staple for decades, and the wording and punctuation shift from one telling to the next. Every version credits Lenin, and none comes with a citation to his writings.

items.why: The Overstreets went through Lenin’s Selected Works and found nothing like it. Stanford researchers and the curator of the Library of Congress Slavic Room also failed to authenticate it (Boller & George, pp. 70–72 ↗).

Some versions date the quote to 1924. Boller & George point out that Lenin died in January 1924 after a long illness, so a new plan for world conquest that year is very unlikely (They Never Said It ↗).

Wikiquote ↗ notes that the last two sentences have also been pinned on Khrushchev. Boller & George say that in the 1960s the overripe-fruit line merged with a fake Khrushchev “doses of socialism” quote, which was itself made up in 1960.

Reagan quoted the line in 1985, according to Boller & George. In 1988 a Soviet interviewer told him that specialists had found nothing like it in Lenin, and he still could not name a source (transcript ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The words are not Lenin’s. They first appear in American anti-communist rhetoric of the 1950s; the earliest use we have found is J. Anthony Marcus’s statement to a Senate subcommittee on June 17, 1954 (hearing record ↗), and nobody has found them in Lenin’s works.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The quote packed a whole Cold War fear into three sentences: a patient Soviet master plan that would win without a shot. Senators, a cardinal, members of Congress and eventually a president repeated it in good faith. Each repetition made it seem more authoritative, even though nobody ever pointed to a page in Lenin.

The “ripe fruit” image itself is much older than the Soviet state. Wikiquote ↗ notes that it appears in American debates about Cuba. Examples include John Quincy Adams’s apple-falling-from-the-tree letter of 28 April 1823 and Parke Godwin’s 1854 line, “The fruit will fall into our hands when it is ripe.”
context.pull: “Many questionable quotations from Lenin and Stalin that are floating around in ill-informed anti-Communist circles.” — Louis F. Budenz, as quoted by Boller & George

Anthony Marcus, president of the Institute of Foreign Trade, gives the line in his prepared statement (p. 131) and again in testimony (p. 139), citing 'volume X, Collected Works by Lenin, page 172'; Part 4, session of Thursday, July 15, 1954, Nicholas T. Goncharoff gives it at p. 214. Read in the OCR text and page-mapped djvu XML of the Internet Archive scan (Parts 1-5 bound together)

Wikiquote lists the quote under its 'Misattributed' section, noting Spellman's use at the 1954 American Legion National Convention, the Khrushchev misattribution of the last two sentences, and the Adams 1823 / Godwin 1854 ripe-fruit metaphor

Boller & George, They Never Said It (OUP 1989), pp. 70–72: Overstreets, Stanford and the LoC Slavic Room could not find it; the 1924 date is implausible since Lenin died January 1924; Goncharoff apparently made the first use on July 14, 1954; JBS Blue Book 1958 and Budenz quote; Reagan quoted it in 1985; Khrushchev 'doses of socialism' merger in the 1960s (fabricated 1960).
